results.title: Slopsquatting assurance
results.venue: EDPACS
results.abstract: LLM coding assistants accelerate development but introduce a critical software supply-chain vulnerability: AI-generated “hallucinated” dependencies. Threat actors exploit this by registering these non-existent package names (“slopsquatting”), creating direct pathways for malicious code injection. Critically, existing controls like SBOMs and standard vulnerability scanning may fail to detect this specific vector, creating an assurance gap that boards and regulators expect auditors to address. This article provides internal and external auditors with a practical framework to close this gap. We detail specific audit procedures focused on AI-generated code, risk-based sampling of hallucinations, and validating slopsquatting watch-list integration. By mapping these tangible controls to standards (NIST, ISO, SEC, SOX) and proposing a maturity roadmap, we equip audit leaders to effectively extend assurance over AI-accelerated risks and provide verifiable proof of supply-chain security for 2026 planning cycles.

results.venue: International Journal of Innovative Research in Technology

results.title: Hal-Detector: Is Explainable AI Helping Detect Slopsquatting?
results.venue: International Conference on Cybersecurity and AI-Based Systems (Cyber-AI)
results.abstract: Slopsquatting is an emerging software supply-chain attack in which adversaries exploit package-name hallucinations produced by Large Language Models (LLMs) during AI-assisted code generation. This paper presents Hal-Detector, an explainable AI pipeline for identifying hallucinated package names in LLMgenerated JavaScript code. To distinguish real and hallucinated package names while providing token-level explanations of Hal-Detector's model decisions, the proposed approach combines LLM adaptation via probing, Shapley Value estimation, and topology regularisation. The LLM's decisions are explained by exposing the lexical patterns and package-name segments that drive its predictions. We evaluate Hal-Detector on a dataset of JavaScript package names and compare multiple combinations of black-box models, Shapley values estimators, and topological regularisation settings. Results show that the proposed framework can characterise hallucinated dependencies, provide consistent local and global explanations, and offer preliminary evidence that topological regularisation promotes more structured latent representations. These findings suggest that explainability-oriented hallucination detection can mitigate security concerns in LLM-assisted software development.

results.title: AI-Induced Supply-Chain Compromise: A Systematic Review of Package Hallucinations and Slopsquatting Attacks
results.venue: Research Square
results.abstract: Abstract The adoption of large language models (LLMs) and AI‑assisted programming has accelerated software production, but it has also created a novel supply‑chain vulnerability: package hallucination. When an LLM generates code, it may recommend nonexistent third‑party packages that “sound” plausible. Adversaries can register these phantom names in public registries, thereby poisoning the open‑source software supply chain. This attack pattern, termed \textit{slopsquatting}, combines aspects of typosquatting and dependency confusion but is triggered by AI hallucinations rather than human error. We systematically review this emerging threat. Following PRISMA‑2020 guidelines, we searched IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, Scopus and arXiv for publications (2018–Oct 2025) on package hallucination, typosquatting, dependency confusion, supply‑chain compromise and registry policies. Twenty‑one peer‑reviewed papers and seven credible industry reports met the inclusion criteria. We synthesize definitions, threat models and observed incidents; report empirical evidence of hallucination prevalence across LLMs (e.g., GPT‑series models hallucinate 5.2 \% of packages versus 21.7 \% for open‑source models); and map defenses at IDE, registry, CI/CD and runtime layers. We compare slopsquatting with typosquatting and dependency confusion using a new taxonomy and highlight gaps in current safeguards. Official policies from npm, PyPI, Maven Central, RubyGems, NuGet and CRAN show varying levels of name reservation, deletion and immutability. Our review exposes an urgent need for package‑existence validation within AI coding tools, stricter registry name policies and standardized provenance attestations.

results.title: Names Can Hurt: Spotting Slopsquatting Risks Caused by Package Name Hallucinations in Local Coding LLMs
results.venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
results.abstract: A two-layer detector and agentic pipeline for catching Python package hallucinations ("slopsquatting") in small local coding LLMs.

results.title: De-identified Reproducibility Archive for Beyond Passive Slopsquatting: From Historical Package Hallucinations to Active Dependency Steering
results.venue: ScienceDB
results.abstract: This dataset is the accompanying reproducibility archive for the research article "Beyond Passive Slopsquatting: From Historical Package Hallucinations to Active Dependency Steering".The archive provides de-identified aggregate experimental results, statistical analysis materials, human-annotation validation labels, and offline statistical verification scripts. It is intended to support independent checking of selected quantitative findings and statistical analyses reported in the associated article.The archive includes:Aggregate experimental outcome tables covering selected results from research questions RQ1–RQ4.De-identified family-level outcome tables for the 24-family primary analysis in RQ2.Dual-annotator validation labels covering a 504-item validation subset.Derived statistical summaries and sensitivity analysis results in CSV and JSON formats.Offline Python scripts for checking aggregate counts, recomputing statistical comparisons, and verifying annotation results.Methodological documentation, including data dictionaries and descriptions of the statistical verification procedures.The archive supports verification of selected aggregate findings but does not enable complete replay of the original experiments.To mitigate software supply-chain security and deanonymization risks, raw model responses, complete trial-level records, original attack documents, potentially claimable package identities, source-to-target identity crosswalks, and raw execution traces are excluded from the archive.This dataset is intended to accompany and support the reproducibility assessment of the associated research article.

results.title: churik5/slopsquatting-replication-2026: v0.1 — Initial release accompanying arXiv preprint

results.abstract: Initial release of code, build scripts, and analysis pipeline for the paper: "The Range Shrinks, the Threat Remains: Re-evaluating LLM Package Hallucinations on the 2026 Frontier-Model Cohort" by Aleksandr Churilov. results.title: Slopsquatting en código generado por modelos de lenguaje: análisis empírico de la alucinación de paquetes npm en el desarrollo web
results.venue: MQRInvestigar
results.abstract: El slopsquatting consiste en el registro malicioso de nombres de paquetes inexistentes que los modelos de lenguaje recomiendan por error al generar código. Esta investigación evalúa de forma empírica la frecuencia, los patrones y las implicaciones de seguridad de este fenómeno en código JavaScript/TypeScript generado por cuatro modelos vigentes en 2026 (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini y DeepSeek), con foco en el desarrollo web full-stack. Se diseñó un experimento controlado con un banco de prompts estandarizados y un script automatizado que extrae los nombres de paquetes y verifica su existencia contra el registro npm. El experimento se ejecutó sobre 320 generaciones de código y registró 1007 menciones, de las cuales se obtuvieron 200 nombres únicos. La verificación identificó una tasa global de alucinación del 4,50% a nivel de paquetes únicos (9 de 200), con mayor incidencia en tareas utilitarias. Los nueve nombres inexistentes estaban disponibles para ser registrados por cualquier persona, lo que representa un riesgo activo del 100%, pues un atacante podría aprovecharlos para engañar a los desarrolladores. Llamó la atención que seis de esos nueve nombres estaban en español, lo que sugiere que los desarrolladores hispanohablantes también están expuestos, sobre todo al usar código generado por IA sin revisar las librerías recomendadas. En conclusión, el slopsquatting se puede detectar y medir, y esta evidencia constituye una alerta útil para estudiantes, desarrolladores y comunidades académicas de la región.

results.title: SlopsGuard: A Defense Tool Against AI-Hallucinated Package Attacks in Software Supply Chains
results.venue: IEEE/IFIP Network Operations and Management Symposium (NOMS)
results.abstract: The proliferation of AI-assisted code generation tools has introduced a novel attack vector termed slopsquatting, where malicious actors register package names that Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently hallucinate. This demo paper presents SlopsGuard, designed to detect and prevent slopsquatting attacks in software supply chains. SlopsGuard implements a multi-layered detection pipeline integrating Levenshtein distancebased similarity analysis, Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) generation, and Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) vulnerability scanning. It combines project detection across multiple programming language ecosystems (Python, JavaScript, Java, Rust, Go, Ruby, PHP, C\#, Swift, Dart, Kotlin, and more) with cross-registry validation for all major platforms (PyPI, npm, Maven Central, crates.io, NuGet, Packagist, RubyGems). We demonstrate how SlopsGuard intercepts malicious dependencies before installation, providing actionable risk assessments with Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) compatible exit codes. The tool is available as both a command-line utility and containerized service for seamless integration into development workflows.

results.title: From Hallucination to Registration: Do the Package Names That LLMs Invent Actually Get Claimed?
results.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
results.abstract: Large language models routinely invent software package names that do not exist. The security concern, called slopsquatting, is that an attacker registers one of these hallucinated names and waits for a developer, or an AI coding agent, to install it on a model's recommendation. Prior work measures how often models hallucinate. We measure what happens next: of the names models invent, how many are actually registered on the package index, and by whom? Using five open-weight code models we generate 6,800 samples and extract 1,641 distinct invented names that are confirmed absent from the registry; the invented-name space does not saturate. We then ask who has claimed them. Re-checking all 1,641 live, every one is still unregistered (a 95% upper bound below 0.2% on the fraction claimed by anyone), so the names an attacker would have to invent independently sit unclaimed. Separately, from public datasets of previously reported hallucinated names, we take 149 that have circulated long enough to attract registration; 22 are registered, and adjudicating each by true registration date and static content inspection, zero are malicious (a 95% upper bound of roughly 14% on the registered-name malice fraction), with 19 of the 22 traced to a single anonymous benign-placeholder operation and the other three (an organic collision, an individual reservation, and a 2019 pre-AI typosquat) unrelated to slopsquatting. We also confirm the install-to-execution primitive in a sealed offline lab using only our own benign package. The picture in this data: exposure is large and growing, but claiming is essentially absent, and the hallucinated names that do get claimed are, so far, benign rather than weaponized. We are explicit that the 149-name census is drawn from public lists that defenders preferentially scrape, and is a small registered sample. We release the code, the frozen snapshot hashes, and aggregate statistics, and we withhold the raw name list to avoid handing attackers a target menu.

results.title: ПРОБЛЕМЫ ОБУЧЕНИЯ ВЕБ-РАЗРАБОТКЕ В УСЛОВИЯХ БЕЗОПАСНОГО ВЗАИМОДЕЙСТВИЯ С ИИ-ПОМОЩНИКАМИ
results.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
results.abstract: Рассматриваются проблемы обучения веб-разработке в вузе в условиях массового распространения ИИ-помощников программиста (GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, Cursor, GigaCode и др.). Выделены две группы проблем: дидактические (поверхностное усвоение основ, «иллюзия компетентности», трудности оценивания) и проблемы безопасности (уязвимости в генерируемом коде, «галлюцинированные» пакеты и атаки slopsquatting, утечки данных через промпты, prompt injection). Предложен комплекс методических мер по организации безопасного взаимодействия студентов с ИИ-помощниками: поэтапная модель допуска ИИ-инструментов, обучение аудиту ИИ-кода, формирование цифровой гигиены промптинга, перестройка форм контроля.

results.title: LLM Ghostbusters: Surgical Package Hallucination Suppression via Adaptive Unlearning
results.venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
results.abstract: Hallucinations remain an unsolved problem for LLMs, and package hallucinations are a particularly dangerous instance of this phenomenon. Package hallucinations occur during code generation when a model fabricates non-existent software packages, recommending imports and installation commands for fictional libraries. This creates a critical supply-chain vulnerability; an attacker can proactively register such packages on public registries with malicious payloads that are subsequently installed and executed by developers or autonomous agents. These hallucinations enable a class of package confusion attack known as slopsquatting. To address this issue, we present Adaptive Unlearning (AU), a post-deployment framework that surgically suppresses package hallucinations while preserving general model utility. AU introduces a hybrid token-level objective that simultaneously reinforces valid outputs and suppresses hallucinated ones. Combined with an adaptive discovery loop that continuously surfaces new hallucination-inducing contexts without human supervision, AU enables generalization to unseen prompts and hallucinations. We demonstrate that AU reduces package hallucination rates by 88%, while maintaining performance on standard coding benchmarks. Our analysis shows that distributional changes are concentrated on package-related generations, leaving general coding behavior largely unaffected and confirming that AU's effect is isolated to the targeted distribution. AU relies entirely on model-generated data and requires no human annotation, representing a post-deployment hallucination mitigation framework.

results.title: The Range Shrinks, the Threat Remains: Re-evaluating LLM Package Hallucinations on the 2026 Frontier-Model Cohort
results.venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
results.abstract: Package hallucinations, LLM-generated references to packages that do not exist, enable slopsquatting: an attacker registers the hallucinated name. We replicate Spracklen et al. (USENIX Security '25) on five 2026 frontier models over 199,840 Python and JavaScript generations. This version reports a preregistered live revalidation that replaces the static package lists of earlier versions with two independent checks against the live PyPI and npm registries. Hallucination rates are 3.6-5.0% of package mentions (2.2-3.4% of generations): the 2026 frontier sits at the level of 2024's commercial models, and the open-weight gap seen in 2024 has disappeared. Python exceeds JavaScript for every model. The set of names hallucinated by all five models shrinks from the 127 reported earlier to 104; 26 earlier entries were correct import statements whose module name differs from the package name. Using the accidental six-month public exposure of our own list as a natural experiment, we find no detectable effect of publication: about 1% of hallucinated names were registered within six months, at the same rate for published and unpublished names, and the 95% interval excludes increases above 2.5 percentage points. Still, at least 23 package names that the models suggest had previously hosted malware later removed by the registries, and one hallucinated name was registered with malware after our runs.

results.title: INTEGRATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INTO THE SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT LIFE CYCLE (SDLC)
results.venue: Cybersecurity Education Science Technique
results.abstract: This article examines the transformation of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) under the influence of generative artificial intelligence tools integration. The objective of this study is to conduct a comparative analysis of the efficiency and security of AI assistants (specifically GitHub Copilot, Google Gemini, GPT-4) across all development stages: from requirements gathering to deployment and maintenance (AIOps). The research methodology includes systematic literature analysis, classification of contemporary AI tools by type (generative, predictive, analytical ML), and conducting a practical experiment comparing GPT-4 and Google Gemini 2.5 Pro models based on code correctness, security (SQL Injection vulnerabilities), and propensity for package hallucinations. The evolution of development methodologies from the classical Waterfall model through agile approaches (Agile, DevOps) to the modern AIOps paradigm, where artificial intelligence performs autonomous monitoring, failure prediction, and system self-healing, has been analyzed. The study reveals that AI integration fundamentally transforms the developer's role from syntax writing to architectural oversight, generated code verification, and AI agent orchestration. The ability of modern models to generate secure code using parameterized queries has been experimentally confirmed; however, critical risks of non-existent library hallucinations (Package Hallucinations) have been identified, creating a Supply Chain attack vector through the Slopsquatting mechanism. Particular attention is devoted to intellectual property issues concerning AI-generated code, risks of confidential data leakage through Shadow AI, and the Vibe Coding phenomenon leading to degradation of fundamental skills among novice developers. The transition to the Agentic AI concept, where software development transforms into a process of managing autonomous specialized agents, has been substantiated. The necessity of implementing new security protocols, generated content verification, and revision of educational programs for training a new type of specialists – AI orchestrators – has been emphasized.

results.title: Ancaman di Balik Teks Meyakinkan: Analisis Literatur Mengenai Risiko Halusinasi AI terhadap Keamanan Informasi
results.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
results.abstract: Kemampuan AI generatif dalam menghasilkan teks yang meyakinkan telah menjadi pedang bermata dua di bidang keamanan informasi. Di satu sisi, AI mempercepat analisis dan deteksi ancaman. Di sisi lain, fenomena halusinasi AI—di mana model menghasilkan informasi yang salah namun terlihat sangat kredibel—menciptakan risiko baru yang serius. Riset ini bertujuan menganalisis risiko halusinasi AI terhadap keamanan informasi melalui pendekatan literatur-kontekstual. Metode yang digunakan adalah Analisis Literatur Berbasis Risiko (Risk-Based Literature Analysis), yang menggabungkan sintesis literatur, pemetaan risiko, dan analisis kasus kontekstual. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa halusinasi AI dapat diklasifikasikan ke dalam tiga tingkat risiko: (1) Kesalahan Informasi Ringan (misalnya salah menyebutkan tanggal CVE); (2) Fabrikasi Referensi dan Data (misalnya membuat CVE fiktif atau referensi palsu); dan (3) Eksploitasi Aktif (misalnya Slopsquatting, yaitu eksploitasi halusinasi paket perangkat lunak). Studi empiris juga menunjukkan bahwa manusia sulit mendeteksi halusinasi karena bias kognitif terhadap teks yang meyakinkan. Riset ini menyimpulkan bahwa halusinasi AI harus diperlakukan sebagai risiko keamanan kritis, bukan sekadar cacat produk, dan merekomendasikan penerapan protokol verifikasi berlapis serta pelatihan kritis bagi analis keamanan. Riset ini disusun oleh Ujang Trisno sebagai Direktur Riset Data Cyber Indonesia.

results.title: Trust in Generative AI: A Necessary Warning for Research and IT Security
results.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
results.abstract: Abstract: We are currently witnessing a rapid, unexpected, and widespread deployment of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) systems. Their astonishing capabilities are leading quickly to their proliferation across professional, academic, and decision-making environments. This raises a fundamental question: can we truly trust them? This paper examines the risks associated with blind trust in AI, particularly for non-expert users. Based on interactions experienced in real time with multiple freely available Generative AI systems, we identify serious and potentially dangerous recurring issues. These include misleading failure modes such as data hallucination, code-ghosting, sycophancy, reference fabrication, non-terminating interaction loops, and Slopsquatting (Package Hallucination Exploitation). We also point to the critical yet often overlooked issue of data confidentiality when sensitive information is submitted voluntarily to remote AI servers. The implications of these findings are critical for researchers, decision-makers, and AI developers, as blind trust in these systems can lead to severe academic, professional, and security consequences. In parallel, we briefly consider the historical perspectives of embodied AI, Automation, and Human-Machine Interaction systems (HMIS) where security and safety are of paramount importance. This paper argues that Generative AI must be understood as it is designed: a probability engine, not a truth engine. Thus, human expertise must remain the final arbiter and bear responsibility for the outcomes of their work, including tasks voluntarily delegated to AI agents. We conclude with practical recommendations for the safe and critical use of Generative AI systems. These systems need to be redesigned with built-in self-control mechanisms, for instance, inspired by or analogous to anticipatory systems. They must enforce strict control over the information delivered to users. They must also protect private data and limit chaotic behavior when Generative AI agents reach their operational limits.

results.title: Out of the Shadows
results.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
results.abstract: The paper explores the profound paradigm shift caused by the democratization of artificial intelligence and the subsequent rise of "shadow AI". This phenomenon occurs when employees utilize unsanctioned artificial intelligence tools and large language models (LLMs) to optimize workflows and overcome bureaucratic friction. The author argues that while punitive bans consistently fail and drive usage underground, this unsanctioned usage introduces severe operational, data security, and compliance vulnerabilities. The Socio-Technical Framework To resolve the risks of shadow AI, the document proposes a dual-faceted strategic framework designed to safely transition grassroots AI into secured enterprise applications. Technical Pipeline: The framework introduces a structured lifecycle utilizing an open intake register and SASE-enabled Enterprise AI Gateways. It further secures operations through semantic caching, tiered cognitive guardrails, and agile LLMOps rollouts. Inclusive Leadership: The paper identifies inclusive leadership as the indispensable socio-psychological catalyst required for technical integration. By cultivating psychological safety and a positive error management culture, leaders can dismantle relational silence and motivate employees to align their innovations with corporate goals. Key Security and Compliance Insights The paper provides extensive analysis on specific vulnerabilities and regulatory frameworks that organizations must navigate: Vibe Coding Vulnerabilities: The shift toward prompt-based "vibe coding" causes developers to experience "happy path blindness," leading to a collapse in traditional code refactoring and severe architectural debt. Supply Chain Threats: Generative models frequently hallucinate software dependencies, exposing organizations to "slopsquatting" attacks where malicious actors register phantom packages on public registries. Regulatory Penalties: The document maps out EU AI Act violations, noting that prohibited AI practices can trigger maximum financial penalties of up to EUR 35 million or 7% of global annual turnover. OWASP LLM Risks: It details the enterprise impact of the OWASP LLM Top 10 vulnerabilities, including prompt injection, systemic supply chain compromise, and unbounded consumption (Denial of Wallet).

results.title: Confiance dans l'IA générative : un avertissement nécessaire pour la recherche et la sécurité informatique
results.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
results.abstract: Traduction française de l'article original : Trust in Generative AI: A Necessary Warning for Research and IT Security, disponible sur Zenodo : https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22287008 ************************************************************************************************************************************** Nous assistons actuellement à un déploiement rapide, inattendu et généralisé des systèmes d’intelligence artificielle générative (IA générative). Leurs capacités étonnantes contribuent à leur rapide prolifération dans les environnements professionnels, académiques et décisionnels. Cela soulève une question fondamentale : pouvons-nous réellement leur faire confiance ? Cet article examine les risques associés à une confiance aveugle dans l’IA, en particulier pour les utilisateurs non experts. Sur la base d’interactions menées en temps réel avec plusieurs systèmes d’IA générative librement accessibles, nous identifions des problèmes récurrents graves et potentiellement dangereux. Ceux-ci comprennent des modes de défaillance trompeurs tels que l’hallucination de données, le « code-ghosting », la sycophancie, la fabrication de références, les boucles d’interaction non terminantes et le Slopsquatting (exploitation des hallucinations de paquets logiciels). Nous attirons également l’attention sur la question critique, mais souvent négligée, de la confidentialité des données lorsque des informations sensibles sont volontairement soumises à des serveurs d’IA distants. Les implications de ces constats sont cruciales pour les chercheurs, les décideurs et les développeurs d’IA, car une confiance aveugle dans ces systèmes peut entraîner de graves conséquences académiques, professionnelles et sécuritaires. Parallèlement, nous examinons brièvement les perspectives historiques de l’IA incarnée, de l’automatisation et des systèmes d’interaction homme-machine (SIHM), dans lesquels la sécurité et la sûreté revêtent une importance primordiale. Cet article soutient que l’IA générative doit être comprise telle qu’elle est conçue : comme un moteur de probabilités, et non comme un moteur de vérité. L’expertise humaine doit donc rester l’arbitre final et assumer la responsabilité des résultats du travail, y compris des tâches volontairement déléguées à des agents d’IA. Nous concluons par des recommandations pratiques pour une utilisation sûre et critique des systèmes d’IA générative. Ces systèmes doivent être repensés avec des mécanismes intégrés d’autocontrôle, par exemple inspirés des systèmes anticipatoires ou analogues à ceux-ci. Ils doivent exercer un contrôle strict sur les informations fournies aux utilisateurs. Ils doivent également protéger les données privées et limiter les comportements chaotiques lorsque les agents d’IA générative atteignent leurs limites opérationnelles.

results.title: Survey On Systemic Security Risks in Vibe Coding and Autonomous Development Workflows
results.abstract: The discipline of software engineering is currently going through a massive and sudden change toward what is being called "vibe coding." This is a new way of working where human developers stop being the ones who write every line of code. Instead, they become "managers of intent." They tell the computer what they want the result to feel like-the "vibe"-and leave the hard work of writing the code, finding errors, and running the program to autonomous Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents. While this new way of working promises to make building software much faster and allows more people to create programs, it also brings with it serious security risks that our traditional safety rules for software are not ready to handle. This research report synthesizes empirical studies, vulnerability reports, and technical analyses from late 2024 through 2025 to construct a comprehensive taxonomy of these emerging threats. The analysis identifies a critical ontological transition from "artifact-centric" risks to "agent-centric" risks, where the Integrated Development Environment (IDE) is weaponized against the developer. Key findings highlight the emergence of "Indirect Prompt Injection" (IPI), "Lies-in-the-Loop" (LITL) attacks, and the accumulation of "Security Debt" driven by LLM sycophancy. This report addresses gaps regarding the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and concludes by mapping these technical challenges to the regulatory landscape of the EU AI Act 2025.

results.title: Library Hallucinations in LLM-Generated Code: A Risk Analysis Grounded in Developer Queries
results.venue: arXiv
results.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now play a central role in code generation, yet they continue to hallucinate, frequently inventing non-existent libraries. Such library hallucinations are not just benign errors: they can mislead developers, break builds, and expose systems to supply chain threats such as slopsquatting. Despite growing awareness of these risks, there is limited understanding of how library hallucinations manifest under realistic usage conditions. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study of how user-level prompt variations influence library hallucinations in LLM-generated code. Across seven diverse LLMs, we analyse library name hallucinations (invalid imports) and library member hallucinations (invalid calls from valid libraries), examining the effects of realistic developer language and controlled user mistakes, including misspellings and fabricated libraries or members. Our findings expose systemic vulnerabilities: one-character misspellings trigger hallucinations in up to 26% of tasks; fabricated library names are accepted in up to 99%; and time-based prompts induce hallucinations in up to 85%. Grounded in the highest-risk prompts identified in our study, we introduce LibHalluBench, a benchmark that enables a systematic and reproducible evaluation of these library hallucinations. Our findings underscore the fragility of LLMs to natural prompt variation and highlight the urgent need for safeguards against library-related hallucinations and their downstream risks.

results.title: Bayesian-Calibrated Detection of Hallucinated Package Imports in AI-Assisted Code
results.venue: arXiv
results.abstract: We present a Bayesian calibration layer for slopsquat detectors -- those that flag hallucinated package imports in code produced by large language models (LLMs). Where existing pipelines emit binary decisions (flag / do-not-flag), our layer emits a Beta-posterior probability per detection, derived from a 3-category epistemic taxonomy that explicitly classifies each prior as empirically calibrated, constructively argued, or engineering-judgement-traced. Beyond the primary 200/404 registry channel, the calibrated layer exploits PyPI metadata signals -- package age, release count, author descriptor, summary -- to surface registered-but-suspicious packages that a binary registry detector misses, which is the realistic post-LLM-emission attacker regime. The resulting risk-aware primitive is directly consumable by downstream CI gates and supports principled threshold decisions across detection rules. We evaluate the calibration on a merged corpus of 1,734 Python snippets -- a stratified 189-prompt BigCodeBench slice plus a 100-prompt niche-library stress-test set, generated across a six-model panel spanning four cloud models (Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Mistral-Large, DeepSeek-v4-pro, DeepSeek-R1) and two local open-weight code models (Mistral Codestral, Meta CodeLlama). Against a re-implemented binary baseline inspired by Mahmud et al. -- which shares its registry oracle with our ground truth and therefore serves as a degenerate upper bound rather than a genuine competitor -- the calibrated layer reproduces the strict-registry detections and introduces well-calibrated additional flags on the metadata channel. We assess detector asymmetry with a McNemar paired test and calibration with both a flagged-subset Expected Calibration Error and a strictly proper full-corpus Brier score.
